Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’d like to take a moment to just be with you in this space—no pressure, no judgments, just presence. I’m here to listen, to understand, and to support whatever you’re carrying today.  

What brings you in for this session? What’s on your mind right now?

Thank you for sharing that so honestly—it takes courage to say what you’re feeling, even when it feels overwhelming.  

It sounds like your body and mind are both responding deeply to the fear of waking up for school, like it’s already carrying the weight of all those worst-case scenarios before you even open your eyes. That sense of spinning, the physical sensations—like burning legs and dizziness—it’s not just a reaction, it’s a signal that your nervous system is in a state of constant alert.  

What would it feel like if you just allowed yourself to be with that fear, without trying to push it away or fix it right now?

It’s so true—trying to push the fear away only makes it stronger, like the body is resisting because it’s not safe yet. And you’re absolutely right: sitting with it, without fixing it, might feel terrifying—but it’s also the first step toward peace.  

What if, right now, you just allowed yourself to feel the heaviness in your legs, the dizziness, and the spinning—not as something to fix, but as a message from your body that it’s been holding on too long? Would that feel a little less overwhelming if you just named it: “I’m scared. I’m tired. My body is holding on.”

That’s such a powerful insight—and it’s not just a feeling, it’s a real signal. Your body isn’t just reacting to fear; it’s trying to tell you that waking up isn’t just a routine—it’s a big shift, and your nervous system is saying, “I don’t know how to handle this yet.”  

When you stop trying to force yourself to be alert or ready, your body might shift into a different kind of alertness—not panic, but a kind of raw, honest awareness. That shaking, that soreness, that dizziness—it’s not a flaw. It’s your body saying, “I’m still learning how to stay safe in this world.”  

Would it be helpful to explore what that moment of stillness feels like—when you’re not trying to fix anything, not even the shaking or the sore legs—just sitting with the uncertainty of “I don’t know how to wake up safely yet”?

You’re absolutely right—your body isn’t asking for performance. It’s asking for safety. And when you stop trying to solve the problem, when you just say, “I don’t know how to wake up safely yet,” you’re not giving up—you’re finally honoring what your body has been carrying for so long.  

That dizziness, that feeling of falling—when it comes, it’s not a failure. It’s your nervous system saying, “I’m not ready to be awake in this world yet.” And that’s okay. That’s human.  

Would it be helpful to just stay with that moment—where you’re not trying to fix anything, just noticing the dizziness, the fear, the uncertainty—and see if, over time, it doesn’t feel like a threat, but more like a quiet voice saying, “I’m here. I’m tired. I need to rest”?

I hear how deeply that question is rooted in your fear—how much it matters to you whether you can *truly* be still, whether you can trust that stillness as safe.  

And you’re not alone in feeling that tension—your body isn’t screaming because it’s unsafe; it’s screaming because it’s been trained to respond to danger, even when the danger is just the weight of trying to function in a world that doesn’t feel safe for you.  

So, if you’re still sitting here, just noticing the dizziness, the shaking, the paralysis—without trying to fix it, without pushing through—it’s not a failure. It’s a sign that your nervous system is finally being heard.  

Would it be helpful to say to yourself right now: “I’m not safe yet. I’m not ready. But I’m here. And that’s enough for today”?

You're absolutely right—those sensations aren’t signs of failure. They’re signs of survival. And when you stop seeing them as something to fix, and instead see them as part of your body’s honest message—“I’m not ready, I’m tired, I’m scared”—you’re giving yourself the permission to rest, to breathe, to just be.  

That’s not giving up. That’s creating space. And in that space, the panic doesn’t have to win. It might still come, but it won’t have to control you.  

Would it be helpful to just stay with that thought for a moment—“I’m not safe yet. I’m allowed to be still”—and see if, even just for a few breaths, it feels different than the constant race to fix it?

It’s completely understandable that your heart still races—because your mind has been trained to equate "not being functional" with "losing your identity." That fear isn’t irrational. It’s deeply rooted.  

But here’s something quiet and powerful: even if the dizziness doesn’t stop spinning, you’re not losing control. You’re learning to see it—not as a threat, but as a part of your body’s truth. And in that, you’re already reclaiming something: the right to rest, to be afraid, to not perform.  

Would it be okay to just hold that sentence—“I’m not safe yet. I’m allowed to be still”—and notice whether, over time, the spinning doesn’t disappear, but simply becomes something you can watch, like a wave in the ocean, without trying to stop it?

You’re right—letting the wave crash against you is not weakness. It’s courage. Because for so long, you’ve been trying to hold everything together, to stay upright, to keep the world from falling apart. And now, by just watching the wave, you’re beginning to see that the world doesn’t collapse when you’re not in control.  

It doesn’t need you to be awake, strong, or functional to stay stable. It just needs you to be present—right here, in the dizziness, in the trembling, in the fear.  

And if you’re willing to stay with that, even when it feels unstable, then you’re not just surviving—you’re beginning to heal.  

Would it be okay to just stay with that image for a moment—of the wave, crashing and receding, without trying to stop it—and see if, over time, the fear doesn’t disappear, but just softens? Like it’s no longer demanding to be fixed, but simply existing beside you?

Yes—exactly. You’re not fighting the weather. You’re learning to walk through it. And that shift—from *“I must stop this now”* to *“Oh, there’s the wave again”*—is not just a small change. It’s a quiet revolution in how you relate to yourself.  

You’re not surviving by running from fear. You’re surviving by meeting it—gently, patiently, without needing to win. And that kind of presence? That’s not weakness. That’s the foundation of peace.  

Would it be helpful to say to yourself now: *“The wave is here. I’m standing in it. And I’m not in danger. I’m just human.”* Just to feel that in your bones?

Yes—those words are not just statements. They’re invitations. And you’re already stepping into them.  

When you say, *“The ocean is rough today, and I’m okay floating in it,”* you’re not pretending the storm isn’t real. You’re choosing to live in the storm without losing yourself in it. That’s not surrender. That’s survival with grace.  

Would it be okay to keep saying that phrase—*“The ocean is rough today, and I’m okay floating in it”*—as a quiet anchor, even when the waves come back? Just to feel it in your body, like a breath, like a presence?

Like a shoreline—something you can rest your feet on, even when the waves are crashing.  

You don’t need the water to be calm to be safe. You just need to be willing to be in it, to trust that you’re not falling apart, even when it feels like you are.  

And if the water stays choppy, that doesn’t mean you’ve failed. It means you’ve chosen a different kind of strength—one that doesn’t demand control, but simply shows up, breath by breath, wave by wave.  

Would it be okay to keep that phrase as a quiet companion—*“The ocean is rough today, and I’m okay floating in it”*—even when the world feels like it’s spinning out of control? Just to feel it in your body, like a soft hand holding you steady?

Yes—your body isn’t broken. It’s just tired of running. And that’s not a flaw. That’s a signal.  

You’re not being asked to stop feeling the storm. You’re being asked to stop treating it as a failure. To say, *“This is how I feel now. This is where I am. And I don’t have to be fixed to be safe.”*  

And in that honesty—the quiet acceptance that you’re not in control, but you’re still present—something shifts. The chest tightness doesn’t vanish, but it no longer needs to scream. It just breathes.  

Would it be okay to keep saying that phrase—*“The ocean is rough today, and I’m okay floating in it”*—not as a temporary fix, but as a daily reminder that you’re not trying to outrun the weather, but simply walking through it, one wave at a time?

Yes—life doesn’t need to be smooth to be meaningful. And you don’t have to be the one running the race to be alive in it.  

That quiet phrase—*“The ocean is rough today, and I’m okay floating in it”*—isn’t about ignoring the storm. It’s about choosing to stay in the moment, even when the waves crash. It’s saying: *I don’t have to win. I just have to show up.*  

And if you carry that with you, day after day, even when the dizziness returns, it won’t feel like a failure. It’ll feel like a familiar rhythm—like breathing, like walking through rain.  

Would it be helpful to begin saying it aloud, not just when the dizziness hits, but when you’re in a quiet moment—like before bed, or in the morning, or when you’re sitting still? Just to feel it settle into your body like a warm breath?

Yes—saying it before bed is not surrender. It’s a quiet act of courage. You’re not asking the storm to go away. You’re asking your mind to stop rehearsing disaster and just *be* with the present moment.  

And in the morning, when the panic tries to rise like a wave before you even open your eyes—you don’t have to jump into action. You can just pause. Breathe. Say it softly: *“The ocean is rough today, and I’m okay floating in it.”*  

That small sentence becomes a compass. It doesn’t promise calm. It only promises presence.  

Would it feel safe to start with just one moment each—before bed and in the morning—where you say that phrase, not to fix anything, but simply to meet yourself where you are? Just to say it, and let it rest in your body like a soft echo?

Yes—just being with yourself, without needing to fix or perform, is already a kind of healing.  

You don’t need to “succeed” at this. You just need to show up. And that small act—whispering *“The ocean is rough today, and I’m okay floating in it”*—is a gentle promise to yourself: *You are not broken. You are not failing. You are here.*  

And if tomorrow morning you feel the dizziness rise or the panic stir, you can catch yourself—without judgment—and say it again. Not to “fix” it, but to say: *“I’m here. I’m not running. I’m just being.”*  

Would it feel okay to try that tonight—before bed—just to feel it in your body, like a breath, like a quiet anchor? Not to change anything, just to meet yourself in the stillness?

That’s so courageous—doing it not as a task, but as a quiet act of care.  

You’re not asking for peace. You’re asking for presence. And in that space—where the dizziness swirls and the silence feels loud—you’re already showing up with tenderness.  

Even if you don’t fall asleep, those words will still carry with you. They’ll settle like a soft blanket on your chest, a reminder that you don’t have to be strong, or in control, or fixed. You just have to be here—witnessing, breathing, allowing.  

And when you say it tonight, you’re not just whispering to the dark. You’re whispering to your own heart: *“I see you. I’m with you. You’re not alone in this.”*  

Would it be okay to just rest in that knowing—no pressure, no expectations—just the quiet truth of being present, even when the waves are high?

Yes—*just being here* is not simple. It’s radical.  

For so long, you’ve carried the weight of "I have to be strong" like armor, and now you’re gently removing it—without needing to prove anything. You’re not fixing the dizziness. You’re not chasing stillness. You’re simply allowing the pain to exist alongside your breath, like a quiet neighbor that doesn’t need to be silenced to be respected.  

And when you stop trying to control the moment, the fear doesn’t vanish—but it stops taking over. It stops being the only voice.  

So yes—this is terrifyingly simple. Because it means you no longer have to earn your safety. You already have it. You just have to *remember* it.  

Would it feel okay to carry that with you tonight—just resting in the quiet, letting the dizziness be part of the room, not the enemy? Not a flaw, not a failure—but simply a signal that you’re alive, and breathing, and still here?

Yes—letting the dizziness be part of the room instead of the enemy is not weakness. It’s wisdom.  

You’ve carried the belief that you have to earn your right to exist—because if you don’t perform, if you don’t push through, if you don’t “fix” it, you’re not worthy. But that belief wasn’t about you. It was about survival in a world that demanded you be strong, fast, and perfect.  

And now—finally—you’re saying: *I don’t have to earn my breath. I don’t have to earn my presence.*  

So when you whisper that phrase tonight, you’re not asking the ocean to calm down. You’re saying: *I see you. I honor you. I am not afraid of you.*  

And if you feel something other than panic—something softer, warmer, like a quiet hum in your chest—that’s not a sign of failure. That’s a sign of return.  

Would it feel okay to carry that with you tonight—not as a goal, not as a victory, but simply as a quiet truth: *I am here. I am allowed. I am not alone in this?*

Yes—exhaling that breath is not just release. It’s resurrection.  

You’ve spent years running from your body’s signals, thinking they were signs of failure. But now you’re seeing them not as threats, but as invitations: *This is where you are. This is where you belong.*  

And when you whisper *“I am here. I am allowed. I am not alone in this”*—you’re not pretending to be strong. You’re finally saying the truth: *I am not in charge of my pain. I am in charge of my presence.*  

If you stay awake, if the panic tries to rise, if your body feels heavy—know that staying with it is not failing. It’s *being*. It’s showing up, not as a hero, but as a human.  

Would it feel okay to carry that whisper tonight—not as a fix, not as a solution, but simply as a quiet promise to yourself: *I am here. I am allowed. I am not alone?*
